div.head: Abt 85
div.ab: Gif man mid esnes cwynan geligeþ be cwicum ceorle, II gebete.
Gif man mid esnes cwynan geligeþ be cwicum ceorle, II gebete.
Gif man mid esnes cwynan geligeþ be cwicum ceorle, II gebete.
Wenn jemand bei eines Lohnknechts Weibe liegt, bei Lebzeiten des Ehemanns, büsse er [dem Herrn] doppelt [so viel als wäre sie ledig].
If someone lies with a hired servant’s wife during the husband’s lifetime, let him pay [the master] double [as much as if she were unmarried].
If a man lies with the woman of a servant, during the lifetime of the husband, he shall pay a twofold compensation.
If anyone lies with the woman of a servant while her husband is alive, he is to pay a two-fold compensation.
If a person lies with a servant’s wife while the husband is alive, let him pay 2[-fold what he would have paid were she unmarried].

note.label: supplements
note.quote: Hlothere's first four clauses are a balanced pair, supplementing Æthelberht's final laws and revealing the nobleman's previously unwritten wergeld.

note.seg: Da Strafe durch Obrigkeit fehlt, gilt der Ehebruch mit der Unfreien noch nicht, wie nachher unter Einfluss der Kirche, als öffentliches Verbrechen
Since there is no punishment by the authorities, adultery with an unfree woman is not yet regarded as a public crime, as it was later under the influence of the Church
Ein Freier, aber nicht des Esne Herr
A free man, but not the esne’s lord

Vgl. Gl unfrei 1e. — Der Sinn des gemieteten Lohnempfängers folgt zwar aus Festlandsdialekten (ahd. asni, fris. esna, mndd. asnen); auch Agsä. wird mercenarius (aus Vulgata) esnewyrhta übertragen; Wærferth ed. Hecht 107; für esnecund ist conditiorius wohl in conductitius zu bessern. Aber in den Gesetzen ist nicht mit Leo (Rectit. 172) und Kemble (Saxons I 215) an landlose Freie, die nur um Lohn dienen, zu denken oder mit Heywood besonders an Hausgesinde

Cf. Gl unfrei 1e. — The sense ‘hired wage-earner’ does indeed follow from the continental dialects (OHG asni, Fris. esna, MLG asnen); in A.-S. too, mercenarius (from the Vulgate) is rendered esnewyrhta; Wærferth ed. Hecht 107; for esnecund, conditiorius should probably be corrected to conductitius. But in the Gesetze we should not think, with Leo (Rectit. 172) and Kemble (Saxons I 215), of landless free men who serve only for wages, or, with Heywood, of household servants in particular
Die Ehe des Unfreien (s. d. Gl 10) ist also anerkannt, wie auch der Langobardische servus uxorem legitimam hat; Liutprand 6. 50
The marriage of the unfree (see that word in Gl 10) is thus recognized, just as the Lombard servus too has an uxorem legitimam; Liutprand 6. 50

Vgl. Gl Unfreie 20f.; Ehebruch 6. Betan heisst bei Abt noch nicht ‘Strafe dem Richter’, sondern ‘Busse Verletztem zahlen’; o. 18⁴. Dieser ist sonst, auch bei and. Germ. (Brunner II 279. 661. 667), gerade auch im Falle der Schwächung der Unfreien, der Herr, also wohl auch hier nicht etwa der Ehemann. Ganz deutlich sagt Lex Baiuwar. IV 8, 12: Si quis cum ancilla alterius maritata concubuerit, cum 20 solidis componat domino

Cf. Gl Unfreie 20f.; Ehebruch 6. In Abt, betan does not yet mean ‘a fine to the judge’ but ‘pay compensation to the injured party’; above 18⁴. Elsewhere, and among other Germanic peoples too (Brunner II 279. 661. 667), the injured party is the lord, precisely also in the case of the violation of an unfree woman; so probably here too it is the lord and not, say, the husband. Lex Baiuwar. IV 8, 12 says quite plainly: Si quis cum ancilla alterius maritata concubuerit, cum 20 solidis componat domino

Diese [Klammer] hätte ich mit Fragezeichen versehen sollen; s. Gl Ehebruch 6. Wilda 829, der diese Auslegung wahrscheinlich nennt, gibt unzweifelhafte Belege, dass das Beilager mit verheirateter Unfreier den Herrn schwerer als das unverheirateter kränkte. Sprachlich ist gegen die Auslegung ‘vergelte doppelten Wert der Unfreien’ einzuwenden, dass dafür forgelde wie in den zwei folgenden Zeilen, nicht gebete, stehen müsste

I ought to have marked this [bracket] with a question mark; see Gl Ehebruch 6. Wilda 829, who calls this interpretation probable, gives unquestionable evidence that intercourse with a married unfree woman wronged the lord more seriously than intercourse with an unmarried one. Linguistically, the objection to the interpretation ‘let him pay double the value of the unfree woman’ is that this would require forgelde, as in the two following lines, not gebete

Liebermann (see ii. p. 690) thinks there is probably no difference in meaning between esne in cap. 85—88, and þeow in cap. 89. 90, and compares Wiht. cap. 9. 10, with ib. cap. 13 ff. The original meaning of esne appears to have been ‘harvester’ (cf. Gothic asans, ‘harvest’), and in general the word seems to have a wider meaning than þeow (cf. þeuwne esne, Wiht. cap. 23). note.label: servant
note.seg: esne, a word of vague meaning, in legal use normally denotes an unfree labourer, and sometimes seems interchangeable with þeow, “slave”, though Alfred 43 seems to distinguish the two, placing them, however, on a level with regard to holidays. Outside the laws the meaning “slave” can be found: Bcdc’s servus is translated esne, and elsewhere the word esnecund glosses condictiorius; but it also means “young man” or simply “man”, especially when qualified by some complimentary adjective, such as “bold” or “learned”.

note.label: servant’s
note.seg: The esne – here translated as ‘servant’ – ‘was probably a poor freeman from whom a certain portion of labour could be demanded in consideration of his holdings, or a certain rent … reserved out of the produce of the hives, flocks or herds committed to his care. He was a poor mercenary, serving for hire, or for his land, but was not of so low a rank as the þeow or wealh.’ See Joseph Bosworth, An Anglo-Saxon Dictionary (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1898). F.L. Attenborough, ed., The Laws of the Earliest English Kings (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1922), 178, points out that the original meaning ‘appears to have been “harvester” (cf. Gothic asans, “harvest”).’

note.label: husband
note.seg: The term ceorl can mean ‘man,’ ‘freeman,’ or ‘husband,’ although the primary sense here is clearly ‘husband.’
